name: Oregano

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: light, sandy, gritty, or loamy soil with sharp drainage
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Oregano likes light, sandy or loamy soil that drains fast.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: average loam or shallow rocky soil that drains freely
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Average loam or shallow rocky soil is fine, as long as it drains well.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: heavy or wet clay that stays soggy around the roots
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy or wet clay is a problem because it stays soggy around the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Oregano is a Mediterranean herb that does best in poor, dry ground; it dislikes wet, poorly drained soil, where root and stem rot set in and the flavor turns weak. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed or mound for drainage rather than feeding the soil.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Oregano likes poor, dry, well-draining soil and full sun. That sounds backward, but it comes from the dry Mediterranean hills, so rich, damp soil actually makes it weak, rot-prone, and bland. If your soil is heavy clay, plant oregano in a raised bed or mound so water drains away fast, and skip the compost.

ph.note_seasoned: Oregano prefers a near-neutral to slightly alkaline soil, roughly pH 6.5 to 7.5, and tolerates ground from about 6.0 up to 8.0. It is intolerant of acidic soil, so on sour ground a light addition of garden lime helps. As with most herbs, sharp drainage matters more than hitting an exact pH.
ph.note_beginner: Oregano likes soil that is neutral to a little bit chalky, about pH 6.5 to 7.5, and copes anywhere from 6.0 to 8.0. It does not do well in acidic soil, so if your soil is sour, a small amount of garden lime nudges it where oregano wants it.

tip_seasoned: Treat oregano lean and dry: full sun, well-drained soil, infrequent water, and almost no feeding. Overwatering and rich soil are the top killers and the surest way to dull the flavor. Pinch it back for bushy growth, harvest often, and pinch or cut off the flower buds to keep the leaves at their most pungent. Oregano spreads by creeping stems and self-sown seed, so contain it in a pot or with edging and deadhead before it seeds.
tip_beginner: The trick with oregano is to not fuss over it. Give it the sunniest, best-draining spot you have, water it only when the soil dries out, and do not feed it much. Pinch the tips to keep it bushy, snip it often, and pinch off the flower buds to keep the leaves tasting their best. Oregano spreads fast by creeping roots and dropped seed, so grow it in a pot or use edging, and cut the flowers before they set seed.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, or a light annual feed
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Oregano has low fertility needs and is easy to over-feed. A little compost worked in at planting, or at most one balanced feeding a year, is plenty; lean soil gives the best flavor. Over-fertilizing pushes soft, leafy growth at the expense of the concentrated oils that make oregano pungent, and rich soil dulls the taste.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Oregano barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer works against it. A little compost mixed in when you plant, or a single light feeding once a year, is enough. Feed it heavily and you get lots of soft leaves with weaker flavor.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: N/A. Oregano is not fed by N-P-K targets; the goal is lean soil and minimal feed, so no fertilizer analysis applies. At most, one annual application of a balanced general-purpose fertilizer.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: N/A. There is no fertilizer number to hit here, since the aim is to feed oregano as little as possible.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: At most a little compost at planting, or one balanced feeding per year.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little compost at planting, and usually nothing after that.

companions.note_seasoned: Oregano pairs naturally with other sun-loving, low-water Mediterranean herbs that share its lean, well-drained conditions, such as thyme, rosemary, sage, and lavender; group these together so one dry, waterwise bed suits them all, and their flowers draw bees and butterflies. Oregano is also a traditional companion in the vegetable garden, where growers have long planted it near cabbage-family crops in the belief its aroma helps deter cabbage pests. Keep it away from thirsty, rich-soil plants whose watering would rot it, and remember it spreads, so give it its own edge or container rather than crowding slower neighbors.
companions.note_beginner: Plant oregano next to other plants that also like full sun and dry soil, such as thyme, rosemary, sage, and lavender. Many gardeners also tuck it near cabbage and its relatives, believing the scent helps keep pests away. Keep oregano away from plants that need a lot of water, because that wet soil will rot it. Remember that oregano spreads, so give it room at the edge of a bed or grow it in a pot.

good_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, spreading Mediterranean herb with the same full-sun, lean-soil, low-water needs, so it shares a dry bed with oregano without forcing the wet conditions that rot it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Thyme and oregano are both drought-tolerant Mediterranean sub-shrubs wanting full sun and sharp drainage, so co-cultivating them lets one waterwise bed serve both. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility, not a measured pest or yield effect.

good_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean herb that thrives on the same lean, dry, sunny conditions, making it an easy dry-border companion for oregano.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rosemary shares oregano's full-sun, well-drained, low-water requirements, so the pairing is sound co-cultivation in one dry bed. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility.

good_seasoned.name: Sage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Another woody Mediterranean herb with matching lean-soil and low-water needs; it and oregano make a natural, drought-tolerant herb grouping.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Garden sage wants the same full sun, sharp drainage, and lean water as oregano, so co-cultivation is straightforward. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility.

good_seasoned.name: Lavender
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean sub-shrub that wants the identical lean, dry, sharply drained conditions as oregano and draws the same pollinators; the two are classic dry-garden partners.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Lavender and oregano are both Mediterranean sub-shrubs demanding full sun, sharp drainage, and low water, and both are strong pollinator draws, so they co-cultivate well in a dry bed. traditional/medium: shared-conditions plus pollinator benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage and other brassicas
good_seasoned.timing: plant nearby in the vegetable bed
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional companion pairing: growers have long set aromatic oregano near cabbage-family crops in the belief its scent helps discourage cabbage pests. Framed as tradition, not a measured effect, and the soil-moisture needs differ, so site oregano at the dry edge of the bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic herbs including oregano are a long-standing folk companion for the cabbage family, said to deter cabbage moths and worms. This is grower tradition rather than a documented trial, and brassicas want richer, moister soil than oregano, so the cultural match is loose; flagged at low confidence.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Likes the same sunny, dry spot as oregano.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same shared-conditions co-cultivation basis as the good_seasoned Thyme entry. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Thyme is a natural oregano partner because it asks for the same things: full sun, lean soil, and not much water. Grow them together and you can run one dry, waterwise bed rather than a watering compromise, which is what keeps both from rotting at the roots. They also look at home together as a low, fragrant herb patch.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Another sun-and-dry-soil herb that grows happily beside oregano.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Rosemary. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Rosemary wants the same dry, sunny, well-drained conditions as oregano, so the two share a bed with no fuss. Keeping them together means you water the whole group sparingly, which is exactly what oregano needs to stay healthy and full-flavored.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Shares oregano's love of sun and dry soil.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Sage. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sage is a tough Mediterranean herb that likes the same lean, dry, sunny spot as oregano, so the two make an easy, drought-tolerant pairing. Group them and you can keep the watering light for both, which is the key to good flavor and healthy roots.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lavender
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Loves the same dry, sunny conditions and brings in pollinators.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Lavender. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lavender and oregano are classic dry-garden partners: both come from the Mediterranean and want full sun, sharp drainage, and very little water, so one lean bed suits them both. Both also draw bees and butterflies when they flower. Plant them together in free-draining ground and resist the urge to pamper either.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage and other brassicas
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A traditional pairing; many gardeners plant oregano near cabbage to help keep pests off.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same traditional folk-companion basis and soil-moisture caveat as the good_seasoned brassicas entry. traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Setting fragrant oregano near the cabbage family is an old companion-planting habit, the idea being that its strong scent helps confuse or deter cabbage moths and worms. Treat this as grower tradition rather than proven fact. One honest caveat: cabbages want richer, moister soil than oregano's lean, dry ideal, so plant oregano at the dry edge of the bed rather than in the heart of it.

bad_seasoned.name: Basil and other thirsty herbs
bad_seasoned.timing: keep in a separate, wetter bed
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Basil and similar moisture-loving herbs want steady water and richer soil, the opposite of oregano's lean, dry, sharply drained ideal. Grown together, the watering that keeps basil happy keeps oregano's roots too wet and invites rot, so give them separate conditions.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Basil is a tender annual needing consistent moisture and fertile soil, while oregano demands lean, dry, sharply drained conditions; the watering regimes are incompatible and the wetter one drives oregano toward root rot. mechanistic/medium: a clear cultural-conflict rationale, not a documented trial.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on tender new growth, most likely on young seedlings or stressed, crowded plants. Mature oregano's aroma tends to repel them, so this is usually a minor, early-season problem.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small soft bugs grouped on new growth, usually on young seedlings or stressed plants. Grown oregano's scent tends to keep them away, so this is normally minor.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find oregano, mainly at the seedling stage. Oregano has few pests overall and is typically grown with little or no pesticide.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes appear, mostly on young plants. Oregano has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water, and use insecticidal soap or neem if numbers climb. A hard harvest removes much of the infested growth at once.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, and use insecticidal soap or neem if there are a lot. Cutting the plant back also removes most of them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun, lean soil, and good spacing for airflow, and avoid overwatering. Vigorous, unstressed oregano rarely attracts aphids, and mature plants largely deter them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep oregano in full sun with room around it, dry lean soil, and not too much water. Healthy, mature plants rarely get aphids.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellowing on the leaves with faint webbing on the stems, most likely in hot, dry weather or on stressed or indoor plants. Oregano is generally pest-resistant, so this is usually minor and weather-driven.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny yellow speckles on the leaves and faint webbing on the stems, usually in hot, dry weather or on indoor plants. Oregano rarely has pest trouble, so this is normally minor.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-feeding mites that flare in hot, dry conditions and on plants grown indoors. Oregano has few pests overall and seldom needs treatment.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small sap-sucking mites that show up in hot, dry spells or indoors. Oregano has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse plants with a strong spray of water, and use insecticidal soap if numbers build. A hard harvest or shear removes much of the infested growth.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, and use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Cutting the plant back also removes most of them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun and good airflow, and do not let container plants bake bone-dry in a heat wave. Vigorous, unstressed oregano rarely attracts mites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep oregano in full sun with room around it, and do not let potted plants dry out completely in a heat wave. Healthy plants rarely get mites.

diseases.name: Root and stem rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gradual wilting, yellowing, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with brown or black decay at the base of the stems and roots. It is the main way oregano is lost and is tied to wet, poorly drained soil and excess winter moisture rather than to cold.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant slowly wilts, yellows, and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with dark, rotted stems and roots at the base. This is the main thing that kills oregano, and it comes from soggy soil, not cold weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne root and stem rots that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and stem base. Waterlogged ground and wet winters, not cold, are the underlying cause; oregano is intolerant of wet feet.
diseases.cause_beginner: Rots that take hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base of the stems. The real cause is wet soil, not cold, and it is worst over a wet winter.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown and roots are rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus everything on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, keep plants on the dry side, and never let oregano sit in wet ground or excess winter moisture. On clay or in humid regions, use a mound or raised bed and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in fast-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and never let oregano sit in soggy ground, especially over winter. On heavy clay or in humid areas, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots and orange or brown powdery pustules on the leaves and stems, a rust fungus that can spread through a planting if left unchecked. Caught early, pruning off affected parts can save the plant.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small round spots and rusty orange or brown powder on the leaves and stems. This is a rust disease, and if you catch it early, cutting off the affected parts can save the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A rust fungus favored by damp, crowded, poorly ventilated conditions and overhead watering. Oregano can be affected when the foliage stays wet.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus that likes damp, crowded plants and wet leaves. Oregano can catch it when the foliage stays wet.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy affected growth promptly, improve airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. Severely infected plants are best removed to protect the rest.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away the affected parts, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. Badly infected plants are best pulled out.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air circulation, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and remove plant debris. Good airflow and dry foliage are the main defenses.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. Keeping the foliage dry and the area tidy is the main thing.

diseases.name: Botrytis and humid-weather foliar disease
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Grayish moldy patches, spotting, or a powdery-white coating on the foliage, favored by warm, humid, still air and on crowded or overhead-watered plants. A minor issue next to root and stem rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Grayish mold, spots, or a powdery white film on the leaves in warm, humid weather, more likely on crowded plants. A minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi such as Botrytis (gray mold) and powdery mildew that are favored by humidity, crowding, and poor air movement. Oregano is fairly disease-resistant, so these are mainly a humid-climate and overcrowding issue.
diseases.cause_beginner: Leaf fungi like gray mold and powdery mildew that like damp, still, humid air and crowded plants. Oregano is fairly disease-resistant, so this is mostly a humid-weather problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected foliage, open up airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. A hard harvest or shear clears and renews the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off affected leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. Cutting it back also helps.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for air circulation, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and favor upright culinary types over dense low ones where humidity is high. Good airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. In humid areas, more open upright plants handle it better than dense low mats.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. Water new plants until they are established, then let the soil dry between waterings; mature oregano needs little water and is quite drought-tolerant. Container plants dry faster and need checking, but should still dry out between drinks.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not often. Water a new plant until it settles in, then let the soil dry out before watering again. An established oregano needs very little water. Pots dry faster, so check them, but still let them dry between waterings.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to settle new plants while establishing; once mature, only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells. Keep plants on the dry side to avoid root and stem rot.
watering.amount_beginner: A regular soak for a new plant, then much less once it is established.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings. Avoid wetting the foliage, which invites rust and rot in humid conditions.
watering.method_beginner: Pour water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, and let it dry out before watering again. Wet leaves and a soggy base are what make oregano rot.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting or dieback of whole shoots, and a plant that fails despite watering signal too-wet roots and likely root or stem rot, not drought. Flavor also weakens in soft, over-watered growth.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If leaves yellow and shoots wilt or die back even though you are watering, the problem is almost always too much water, not too little. Soggy roots rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Established oregano rarely shows true drought stress; light wilting in extreme heat that recovers overnight is normal and not a reason to increase watering.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Oregano almost never gets too little water once established. A little droop on a very hot afternoon that bounces back by morning is fine.

schedule_by_stage.rate: a regular soak to settle new plants
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The first season is the only time regular watering matters: water new oregano until it is established, then let the soil dry between waterings. Water at the base and keep the foliage dry against rust and rot in humid conditions.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water a new oregano regularly until it settles in, then let the soil dry out before watering again. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry.

schedule_by_stage.rate: occasional deep watering in dry spells
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Mature oregano needs little water and is quite drought-tolerant: only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells, letting the soil dry between drinks. The most common way to kill it is overwatering, and its flavor also weakens in soft, over-watered growth, so keep it on the dry side. Container plants dry faster and need checking, but should still dry out between waterings.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Mature oregano needs very little water. Give it an occasional deep drink only in a long dry spell, and let the soil dry between waterings. Too much water not only rots it but also weakens the flavor. Pots dry faster, so check them, but still let them dry out between waterings.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through dormancy oregano wants very little water; keep it on the dry side and do not let the crown sit in wet winter soil.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter oregano needs almost no water. Keep it on the dry side and never let it sit in soggy soil.

watering.method_note_seasoned: The most common way to kill oregano is overwatering. When in doubt, water less.
watering.method_note_beginner: Remember: more oregano dies from too much water than too little.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters; taper off sharply once the plant is established.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water fairly regularly the first year while it gets established, then back off a lot.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Nursery transplants are already hardened; set them out after the last spring frost. Divisions and rooted cuttings should be hardened gradually before planting out.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you buy a plant from a nursery, you can put it straight in the ground after your last spring frost. There is no seed-starting step you must do.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Oregano is most reliably started from a nursery transplant, a division of an established clump, or a softwood cutting; all can be done in spring. It also grows readily from seed (germinating in about four days in warm soil), but the tiny seed needs light to germinate so should not be covered, and seed-grown plants vary in flavor and do not come true, so named culinary types like Greek oregano are propagated vegetatively. Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before the last frost.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easy, reliable way to grow oregano is to buy a small plant, divide an existing clump, or root a cutting in spring. You can grow it from seed, but the seed is tiny and needs light (do not cover it), and seed-grown plants vary in flavor, so for good culinary oregano most gardeners start from a plant. If you do start from seed, sow it indoors about 8 weeks before your last frost.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering; oregano must never sit in standing water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A gritty, fast-draining potting mix, not a moisture-holding one.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in coarse sand or perlite so water runs straight through.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A coarse, free-draining potting medium; avoid peat-heavy moisture-retentive mixes.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Add coarse sand, perlite, or fine gravel to sharpen drainage.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check the soil, but still let it dry between waterings and never leave the pot standing in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container oregano needs only a very light feed, if any; do not over-fertilize.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In the coldest zones, or with a less hardy type like Greek oregano, grow it in a pot you can move into an unheated but sheltered spot for winter, then bring it back out in spring. A sunny indoor windowsill also works for a winter supply.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Where the chosen type is not reliably hardy, a container lets you overwinter the plant under cover (an unheated garage or porch) or on a bright windowsill; keep it on the dry side and protected from hard freezes, then return it outdoors after frost.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: A container is the recommended way to grow oregano for most gardeners: it suits the plant's love of drying out between waterings and, just as important, it contains oregano's vigorous spread by creeping stems and self-sown seed. Use a wide, free-draining pot with a gritty mix, keep it in full sun, and never let it stand in water. A pot is also the easy way to overwinter less hardy types where winters are cold.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Growing oregano in a pot is a great idea, both because it likes to dry out between waterings and because a pot keeps it from spreading all over the garden. Use a wide pot with holes in the bottom and a gritty mix, keep it in full sun, and tip out any water that collects in the saucer.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers keep the medium too consistently moist for oregano and promote root rot; use a conventional free-draining pot instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for oregano; they keep the soil too wet and the roots rot.

recommended.name: Greek oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9; a touch less cold-hardy than common oregano.
recommended.note: The classic culinary oregano with a hot, spicy, pungent flavor and white flowers; this is the type sold dried in stores and the best pick for cooking.

recommended.name: Italian oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 6 to 9; a milder type often grown as a bring-in plant in cold zones.
recommended.note: A hybrid of oregano and sweet marjoram with large leaves and a milder, sweeter, well-rounded flavor; dries easily and is a versatile kitchen oregano.

recommended.name: Common (wild) oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Very hardy, reliably perennial to about zone 4; the hardiest and most vigorous type.
recommended.note: Also called wild marjoram, this is the toughest and most cold-hardy oregano and the most aggressive spreader, but its flavor is variable and some seed-grown plants are nearly bland, so taste before relying on it for cooking.

recommended.name: Hot & Spicy oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 5 to 9, similar to Greek oregano.
recommended.note: A selection bred for an extra-pungent, peppery kick; a good choice for growers who want the boldest possible oregano flavor.

recommended.name: Golden oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 5 to 9; low and spreading.
recommended.note: A golden-yellow-leaved, variegated form grown as much for its bright foliage as for the kitchen; milder in flavor and lower-growing, it makes an attractive edible groundcover in full sun.

recommended.name: Syrian oregano (za'atar)
recommended.hardiness_note: Tender; hardy only in roughly zones 8 to 10, a bring-in container plant in colder regions.
recommended.note: The traditional za'atar herb, with a distinctive oregano-marjoram flavor used in Middle Eastern blends; more heat-loving and frost-tender than common oregano.

varieties.note_seasoned: Oregano reaches the grower as several practical types. Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) is the hot, pungent kitchen standard and the type sold dried; Italian oregano (O. x majoricum, an oregano-marjoram hybrid) is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano (O. vulgare) is the hardiest and most vigorous but has variable, sometimes bland flavor, so taste before you rely on it. Hot & Spicy is an extra-pungent selection, Golden oregano (O. vulgare 'Aureum') is a bright-foliaged ornamental-culinary form, and Syrian oregano (O. syriacum) is the tender za'atar herb. One important caution: Mexican oregano (Lippia graveolens) is not a true oregano at all but a shrub in the verbena family, grown in hot climates for a similar, stronger flavor. For cooking, start with Greek oregano.
varieties.note_beginner: There are several kinds of oregano. Greek oregano is the bold, spicy one used in cooking and sold dried, and it is the best choice for the kitchen. Italian oregano is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano is the toughest and most cold-hardy, but its flavor varies a lot and some plants are almost bland, so taste it first. Hot & Spicy is extra strong, Golden oregano has bright yellow leaves, and Syrian oregano is the za'atar herb. Watch out for one thing: Mexican oregano is a completely different plant (in the verbena family), not a true oregano, even though it tastes similar. For cooking, start with Greek oregano.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh cut sprigs hold for a few days in a glass of water on the counter. For long-term keeping, dry oregano: unlike most herbs its flavor actually concentrates and improves when dried. Tie small bundles and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, airy place, then strip the leaves into a sealed jar out of the light.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Fresh sprigs last a few days standing in a little water on the counter. Oregano is one of the few herbs that tastes even better dried, so to keep it, hang small bunches upside down somewhere warm and airy, then store the dried leaves in a sealed jar.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh sprigs loosely wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel in a bag, where they keep for about one to two weeks.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep fresh oregano in the fridge, loosely wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel inside a bag, for about one to two weeks.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole sprigs in a bag, or strip the leaves and freeze them in water or oil in ice-cube trays for cooking; frozen oregano keeps its flavor well for months, though drying is the traditional method.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze oregano: put whole sprigs in a bag, or freeze the leaves in water or oil in an ice-cube tray to drop into cooking later.
storage.notes_seasoned: Oregano is one of the sturdy herbs that dries well, and it is unusual in that drying concentrates rather than dulls its flavor. Cut stems for drying just before the plant flowers, when the leaf oils peak, tie them in small loose bundles, and hang them in a warm, dry, airy spot; a paper bag around the bundle keeps off dust. Once dry, strip the leaves and store them sealed and out of the light.
storage.notes_beginner: Oregano is easy to dry, and drying actually makes its flavor stronger. Cut stems just before it flowers, tie them in small loose bunches, and hang them upside down somewhere warm and airy (a paper bag around the bunch keeps the dust off). When dry, rub the leaves off into a sealed jar kept out of the light.

rotation.note_seasoned: N/A. Oregano is a perennial that stays in place for several years, so annual crop rotation does not apply. When replanting an old oregano patch, choose a fresh, well-drained site to avoid carrying over soilborne root rot, and clear any strays it has spread by root or seed.
rotation.note_beginner: N/A. Oregano is not rotated like a vegetable because it is a permanent plant that stays put for years. If you replace an old one, pick a fresh, well-draining spot and pull up any pieces it has spread around.

growth_stages.name: Plant out
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Set the nursery plant, division, or rooted cutting out after the last spring frost, in the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Space plants 10 to 12 inches apart; on heavy ground, plant on a mound or raised bed, and consider a pot or edging to contain the spread.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After your last spring frost, plant the oregano in the sunniest, best-draining spot. Leave about 10 to 12 inches between plants. To keep it from spreading, grow it in a pot or add edging.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A compact young plant with fragrant green leaves and firm roots filling the pot, ready to set out once frost has passed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small bushy plant with fragrant green leaves and roots that hold the potting soil together when you slide it out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen the rootball, set the crown level with the soil surface, and water in once to settle the roots. Do not amend with rich compost or fertilizer; oregano wants lean ground.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Gently loosen the roots, plant so the top of the rootball is level with the soil, and water once to settle it. Skip the fertilizer and rich compost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Planted: type or cultivar, number set out, and the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down which oregano you planted and when.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year one)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first season after planting. Oregano establishes fairly quickly but is still building its root system; pinch the tips once it reaches about 6 inches to encourage branching, and harvest only lightly. It reaches full size by about the second year.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first growing season. Your oregano is settling in and growing roots. Once it is about 6 inches tall, pinch the tips to make it bushier, and only pick a little this year. It fills out by about year two.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new growth spreading low and outward as the plant begins to form a bushy mound. Some spread by creeping stems is normal and healthy.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: New growth spreading low and wide as the plant fills in. It naturally creeps outward a bit, which is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water until the plant is settled, then taper toward infrequent watering. Pinch the growing tips to build a bushy plant, harvest only lightly, and hold off on fertilizer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water fairly often until the plant takes hold, then water less. Pinch the tips to make it bushy, only snip a little, and do not feed it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Establishment: planting-out date, first pinch, and any light harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you planted it and that you pinched it to make it bushy.

growth_stages.name: Spring leaf-out and harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Each spring the plant pushes fresh growth from the base and creeping stems, and this leafy growth is what you harvest through the season by snipping sprigs as needed. Early spring is also the time to cut out any old, leggy wood.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Every spring, new growth appears low on the plant and along its spreading stems. This leafy growth is what you snip through the season for cooking. Early spring is a good time to cut out any old, woody stems.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New soft growth emerging along the stems and crown, signaling the plant came through winter and is growing again. Watch also for new shoots popping up beyond the original clump.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Soft new growth low on the plant in spring. That tells you it survived winter. You may also see new shoots coming up a short way from the main plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut out old leggy wood in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed. Begin harvesting sprigs as needed, settle into infrequent watering, and pull or dig any unwanted spread to keep the plant in bounds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In early spring, once you see new growth and frost is over, cut out any old woody stems. Start snipping sprigs to cook with, water deeply but not often, and pull up any shoots that have wandered where you do not want them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Spring leaf-out: date growth resumed and any spring cleanup done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when spring growth started and if you cleaned it up.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The mid-to-late-summer flowering window, when oregano puts up small clusters of white, pink, or purple flowers that draw bees and butterflies. Leaf flavor is most concentrated just before the flowers open, so many growers pinch or cut the flower buds to keep the leaves pungent and productive.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Mid-to-late summer, when oregano makes tiny white, pink, or purple flowers that bees and butterflies love. The leaves taste best just before it flowers, so many gardeners pinch off the flower buds to keep the leaves strong.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming in clusters on the stem tips. For the strongest flavor and best dried quality, harvest just as the buds form, before they open.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Little flower buds forming in clusters at the tips. For the best flavor, cut sprigs just as the buds appear, before they open.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut sprigs for drying as the flower buds form. Pinch or cut off remaining flowers to favor leaf growth and flavor, or leave some to bloom for pollinators and deadhead before seed sets to limit self-seeding. Keep watering light and do not feed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut sprigs to dry as the buds form. Pinch off the rest of the flowers to keep the leaves tasty, or leave a few for the bees but snip them before they make seed so the plant does not spread everywhere. Keep watering light and do not fertilize.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bloom: bud-formation date, harvest cuts for drying, and whether you removed or kept the flowers.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it started to bud and when you cut oregano to dry.

growth_stages.name: Shear back
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The post-bloom shear, a key upkeep act. After flowering fades, clip the plant back to remove the spent flower stems, tidy the mound, and cut into leafy growth to spur a fresh flush. Deadheading now also limits self-seeding.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The tidy-up trim after the flowers fade. Clip off the spent flower stems and cut the plant back into its leafy growth to bring on fresh new leaves. Trimming now also stops it from dropping seed everywhere.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Spent, browning flower stems and a plant finished with its main bloom. Below the leafy growth are older woody stems that resprout poorly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Faded, brownish flowers and a plant done blooming. Notice the older woody stems below the green growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Shear off the spent flowers and reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth and avoiding the bare old wood. Regular harvesting plus this shear keeps oregano bushy and productive; even so, plants go woody with age and are best divided or replaced every few years.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Trim off the old flowers and cut the plant back into its leafy parts, avoiding the bare woody stems. Snipping often plus this trim keeps oregano bushy, but it still gets woody with age, so replace or divide it every few years.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Shear back: date sheared and roughly how much removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when you trimmed off the old flowers.

growth_stages.name: Dormancy (cold zones)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, oregano dies back to the ground and goes dormant. It needs almost no water, and it is wet soil, not the cold itself, that most often kills it over winter. Where it is at the cold edge of its range, a winter mulch after the ground freezes helps it through.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Where winters freeze, oregano dies back to the ground and rests through the cold months. It barely needs water, and it is soggy soil, not the cold, that usually kills it over winter. In very cold areas, a winter mulch after the ground freezes helps it survive.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Top growth browning and dying back for the season as the plant goes dormant. Roots stay alive underground in hardy zones and push new growth in spring.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The leaves and stems browning and dying back for winter. In hardy areas the roots stay alive underground and grow again in spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop watering and feeding, and leave any hard cutback for spring. At the cold edge of its range, apply a loose winter mulch of straw or evergreen boughs after the ground freezes, and remove it as growth resumes. Move less hardy types or container plants under cover.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering and feeding, and save any big trim for spring. In very cold areas, lay a loose winter mulch of straw over the plant after the ground freezes, and take it off in spring. Bring less hardy types or pots somewhere sheltered.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Dormancy: date growth died back and any winter mulch applied.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it went dormant and any winter cover you added.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your plant-out window is open. Set the nursery plant, division, or cutting in full sun in well-drained soil after the last frost, spacing plants 10 to 12 inches apart. Skip rich compost and fertilizer, and consider a pot or edging to contain the spread.
notifications.body_beginner: It is time to plant your oregano. Put it in a sunny, well-draining spot now that frost has passed, leaving 10 to 12 inches between plants, and do not add fertilizer. A pot helps keep it from spreading.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pinch oregano flower buds for flavor
notifications.body_seasoned: Flower buds are forming. For the most pungent leaves, harvest now just before they open, and pinch or cut off the remaining buds to favor leaf growth. Leave a few to bloom for pollinators if you like, but deadhead before seed sets to limit self-seeding.
notifications.body_beginner: Your oregano is starting to bud. For the best-tasting leaves, snip some now before the flowers open, and pinch off the rest of the buds. You can leave a few flowers for the bees, but cut them before they make seed so the plant does not spread.

notifications.body_seasoned: Blooms are fading, time to shear off the spent flower stems and cut the plant back into leafy growth for a fresh flush. Deadheading now also limits self-seeding. Divide or replace woody old plants every few years.
notifications.body_beginner: Your oregano flowers are fading, so trim off the old flower stems and cut it back into the leafy growth for fresh new leaves. This also stops it dropping seed. Replace or divide woody old plants every few years.

notifications.title_beginner: Get your oregano ready for winter
notifications.body_seasoned: Cold is coming. Stop watering and feeding, leave any hard cutback for spring, and at the cold edge of its range apply a loose winter mulch after the ground freezes. Move less hardy types or container plants under cover. Wet winter soil, not cold, is the usual killer.
notifications.body_beginner: Winter is coming. Stop watering and feeding, save any big trim for spring, and in very cold areas cover the plant with a loose winter mulch after the ground freezes. Bring less hardy types or pots somewhere sheltered. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills oregano.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Late frost on tender new growth
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Late frost on the new growth
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A late spring frost is forecast while the plant is pushing tender new growth. Hold off on any planned cutback until frost has fully passed, and protect newly set-out plants overnight.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A late spring frost is coming while your oregano has soft new growth. Wait to do any trimming until frost is fully over, and cover any just-planted oregano overnight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Humid heat raises rot and rust risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, humid weather raises rot risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A spell of humid heat is forecast, which raises the risk of root rot and foliar disease like mint rust in muggy regions. Do not add water on oregano's account, make sure it is not sitting wet, and keep airflow open around the plant.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, sticky weather is coming, which can lead to rot and leaf disease. Do not give oregano extra water, make sure it is not sitting in wet soil, and keep the area around it open and airy.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Wet winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Soggy winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Prolonged wet soil is forecast heading into or during winter. Wet winter ground, not cold, is what most often kills oregano, so make sure it is not sitting in water and consider moving containers under cover.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A long wet spell is coming around winter. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills oregano, so make sure it is not standing in water, and move pots somewhere protected if you can.

transplant.text_seasoned: Plant oregano lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine, set it in the sunniest, best-draining spot, and on clay build a mound or raised bed. Rich, wet soil weakens flavor and rots the roots.
transplant.text_beginner: Oregano does best in poor, dry soil, so do not add fertilizer or rich compost. Give it your sunniest spot, and if your soil is heavy clay, plant on a little mound or raised bed so water drains away.

transplant.text_seasoned: Contain the spread from the start. Oregano creeps by rooting stems and self-sows, so plant it in a pot, a bottomless bucket sunk in the bed, or behind deep edging if you do not want it colonizing the garden.
transplant.text_beginner: Oregano spreads fast, so decide up front how to contain it: a pot, or edging sunk into the soil, keeps its creeping roots from taking over the bed.

establishment.text_seasoned: Year one is about establishing, not harvesting hard. Water until the plant is settled, then taper off, pinch the tips at about 6 inches to build a bushy plant, and harvest only lightly this season.
establishment.text_beginner: The first year is about getting established. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water less. Pinch the tips when it is about 6 inches tall to make it bushy, and only pick a little this year.

establishment.text_seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Oregano has low fertility needs, and over-fertilizing produces soft growth with weaker flavor. The same goes for water: more is not better and invites rot.
establishment.text_beginner: Try not to feed it. Oregano needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives soft leaves with less flavor. The same is true for water, where more is not better.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Harvest little and often once the plant is established. Snipping sprigs regularly keeps oregano bushy and productive and slows it going woody; you can take leaves anytime for cooking.
vegetative.text_beginner: Once it is established, snip oregano often. Regular cutting keeps it bushy and slows it turning woody, and you can pick leaves anytime to cook with.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Cut out old, leggy wood in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed, and pull up any shoots that have crept beyond where you want them. Cutting into leafy growth, not bare old wood, gives the best regrowth.
vegetative.text_beginner: In early spring, once new growth shows and frost is over, cut out old woody stems and pull up any pieces that have spread too far. Cut into the leafy parts, not the bare old wood.

bloom.text_seasoned: For the strongest flavor, harvest and cut for drying just as the flower buds form, before they open, when the leaf oils peak. Pinch or cut off the flowers to favor leaf growth and keep the best flavor.
bloom.text_beginner: For the best flavor, cut oregano to dry just as the flower buds appear, before they open, when the oils are strongest. Pinch off the flowers to keep the leaves tasting their best.

bloom.text_seasoned: Decide what to do with the flowers. Removing them keeps the leaves at peak flavor and limits self-seeding; leaving some to open feeds bees and butterflies, but deadhead before seed sets so oregano does not sow itself across the garden.
bloom.text_beginner: Decide about the flowers. Cutting them off keeps the leaves tasting best and stops the plant spreading by seed; leaving a few for the bees is fine, but snip them before they make seed.

cut_back.text_seasoned: Shear off the spent flower stems after bloom and cut the plant back into leafy growth for a fresh flush, avoiding the bare old wood. Frequent harvest plus this shear keeps oregano bushy, but it still goes woody with age, so divide or replace it every few years.
cut_back.text_beginner: After it flowers, trim off the old flower stems and cut it back into the leafy parts for fresh new leaves, avoiding the bare woody stems. Snipping often plus this trim keeps oregano bushy, but it still gets woody, so replace or divide it every few years.

cut_back.text_seasoned: Deadhead as you shear to limit self-seeding. Oregano seeds readily and can sow itself across a bed, so cutting the spent flowers before seed matures keeps stray seedlings down.
cut_back.text_beginner: Trim off the old flowers before they make seed. Oregano drops a lot of seed and can pop up all over, so deadheading it as you cut back keeps the seedlings down.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Over winter, do almost nothing: stop watering and feeding, and leave hard cutback for spring. A plant in wet winter soil rots, so the worst thing you can do is keep it watered.
dormancy.text_beginner: In winter, do almost nothing. Stop watering and feeding, and save the trim for spring. Oregano sitting in wet winter soil rots, so do not keep watering it.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Protect plants at the cold edge of the range. In the coldest zones, mulch over the crown with straw or evergreen boughs after the ground freezes and remove it in spring, or overwinter less hardy types like Greek oregano in a pot under cover.
dormancy.text_beginner: Shelter plants in very cold areas. Cover the plant with straw or evergreen branches after the ground freezes and take it off in spring, or grow less hardy types like Greek oregano in a pot you can bring under cover.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature plant yields a steady supply of sprigs through the growing season, easily enough to keep a kitchen stocked with fresh oregano plus bundles to dry; productivity is best once the plant reaches full size at about the second year, and frequent harvesting keeps it coming.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown oregano plant gives you plenty of sprigs all season, enough to cook with fresh and to dry, especially once it is a couple of years old. The more you snip it, the more it makes.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect only light harvests the first year; harvesting sparingly and pinching to build a bushy plant while it establishes pays off in fuller production from the second season on.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect much the first year. Picking lightly and pinching to make it bushy while the plant settles in gives you bigger harvests from year two.
factors_seasoned: Plant age and size (full production at about the second year)
Full sun and lean, well-drained soil
Frequent harvesting and pinching to keep growth soft and non-woody
Removing flowers to keep leaves productive and flavorful

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves turning yellow or the plant dying back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: With oregano, yellowing and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering, poor drainage, and excess winter moisture are the number one killer, leading to root and stem rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: For oregano, yellow leaves and dieback usually mean too much water, not too little. Overwatering and soggy soil are the biggest killer. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back on watering hard and fix drainage. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on clay or in humid areas use a mound or raised bed. Never let oregano sit in wet ground, especially over winter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on heavy or humid ground plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Spreading and taking over the bed
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Oregano spreads by creeping, rooting stems and by prolific self-seeding, so an unchecked plant can colonize a bed and crowd its neighbors. This is the plant behaving normally, not a disease; common wild oregano is the most aggressive.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Oregano spreads on its own, both by creeping roots and by dropping lots of seed, so it can take over a bed if you let it. This is just what oregano does, not a problem with the plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Contain it: grow oregano in a pot or a sunken bottomless container, or set deep edging around it. Deadhead the flowers before seed sets, and each spring pull or dig out shoots that have crept beyond bounds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep it contained: grow oregano in a pot, or put edging around it in the ground. Cut off the flowers before they make seed, and each spring pull up any shoots that have wandered off.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Woody and bare in the middle
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: An oregano plant that has gone woody and bare or open in the center is aging. Oregano goes woody with time; frequent harvest, pinching, and a post-bloom shear slow it, and cutting out old wood at the end of winter helps, but plants are best divided or replaced every few years.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When oregano gets woody and bare in the middle, it is mostly just getting old. All oregano goes woody eventually; snipping often, pinching, and trimming after bloom slow it down, but plants are best replaced or divided every few years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Harvest regularly, pinch to keep growth soft, and shear after bloom, cutting into leafy growth. Cut out old leggy wood at the end of winter, and divide a healthy older clump or start a fresh plant from a cutting every few years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Snip oregano often, pinch the tips, and trim it after it flowers. Cut out old woody stems at the end of winter, and every few years split a healthy older plant or start a new one from a cutting.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Bland oregano with soft, lush growth usually means too much feed, too much water, too little sun, or a seed-grown common type with naturally weak flavor. It can also mean the plant was left to flower, which reduces leaf flavor. The concentrated oils build up in lean, dry, sunny conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Oregano with little flavor usually has too much fertilizer or water, or too little sun, or it is a plain seed-grown type. Letting it flower also weakens the leaf flavor. Oregano tastes strongest when it is grown lean, dry, and sunny.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Stop fertilizing, water less, and give the plant full sun. Choose a named flavorful type like Greek oregano, harvest just before bloom when the oils peak, pinch off flowers, and dry the leaves, which concentrates the flavor.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Stop feeding it, water less, and make sure it gets full sun. Grow a flavorful type like Greek oregano, pick it just before it flowers, pinch off the flowers, and dry the leaves, which makes the flavor stronger.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: N/A. Oregano is a perennial planted once, not a crop sown in succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: N/A. You plant oregano once; you do not resow it through the season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Oregano is a woody perennial harvested continuously from the same plant over several years, so succession sowing does not apply; renew plants by division or cuttings every few years instead.

Hardiness z4 KEPT as DISCLOSED-MODELED (synthesis notes show PSU z5-8 / UF z5-9 transparently; open_finding_001, per Illinois Extension); Italian (majoricum) / Syrian (syriacum) variety hardiness left for the variety-delta pass (generally-safe-now rule).

open_findings.summary: Regional planting/bloom windows are modeled from oregano phenology (mid-to-late-summer bloom: PSU July to September, UF mid-to-late summer, NCSU hirtum late summer) plus each zone's frost dates and the nearest readable T1 guidance, not from an oregano-specific per-region planting chart (none found for all 10 regions). The frost-anchored plant-out windows follow standard set-out-after-last-frost / cool-season-in-hot-climates timing (UF: plant Florida oregano in fall or winter, avoid summer). Windows are generally-safe; tighten exact months at the variety-delta pass.

hardiness_zone_min=4 with northern_tier z4 modeled as a MARGINAL in-ground perennial (winter mulch after the ground freezes per Illinois Extension). Common Origanum vulgare is the hardiest type, rated to about z4 (multiple extension/horticulture sources z4-9); PSU gives z5-8 and UF z5-9, and Illinois calls true oregano marginally hardy in zone 5, so z4 rests on the hardy common type plus sharp drainage and mulch. Greek oregano (the best culinary type) is a touch less hardy (~z5). zone 3 kept annual/container. Confirm at review.

Humid and tropical cells are the lowest-confidence: se_gulf z8-9, fl_peninsula z10-11, and hawaii_tropical z11. NCSU notes oregano is intolerant of hot, humid conditions and prone to root/stem rot and rust in excess moisture; UF/IFAS supports Florida culture with cool-season planting and sharp drainage. fl_peninsula z11 is modeled annual and hawaii as marginal (viable mainly in cooler, drier upcountry microclimates, cited to general oregano culture rather than a Hawaii-specific chart). description_seasoned: Oregano is a spreading, low, woody Mediterranean perennial in the mint family, grown for its pungent aromatic leaves that flavor pizza, tomato sauces, meats, and Mediterranean and Mexican dishes. It forms a bushy, mat-like mound about 1 to 2 feet tall and thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; wet, rich, or humid conditions rot it and dull its flavor. Its flavor peaks just before its mid-to-late-summer bloom, so many growers pinch off the flowers to keep the leaves at their best, and the leaves are unusual in tasting even stronger dried. It is hardy and pest-resistant but spreads by creeping stems and self-sown seed, so it is best contained. Note that Mexican oregano is a different, unrelated plant.
description_beginner: Oregano is a low, spreading herb with pungent, fragrant leaves you cook with, famous on pizza and in tomato sauces. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it does worse if you pamper it. It grows about 1 to 2 feet tall in a bushy mound. The leaves taste best just before it flowers in mid-to-late summer, so many gardeners pinch off the flowers, and oregano is one of the few herbs that tastes even stronger dried. It is tough and rarely bothered by pests, but it spreads by creeping roots and dropped seed, so it is best grown in a pot or with edging. Watch out: Mexican oregano is a different plant, not true oregano.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest oregano sprigs anytime once the plant is established: snip the top few inches of leafy growth, taking up to about three-quarters of the current season's growth at a cutting. Flavor is most concentrated just before the plant flowers, so cut for drying as the buds form, on a dry morning after the dew has lifted. Pinching or cutting off the flowers keeps the leaves pungent, and regular harvesting keeps the plant bushy. Oregano is one of the few herbs whose flavor deepens when dried.
harvest_ready_beginner: You can snip oregano anytime once it is established: cut the top few inches of leafy stems. The flavor is strongest just before it flowers, so that is the best time to cut oregano to dry, in the morning after the dew dries. Pinching off the flower buds keeps the leaves tasting their best, and snipping it often keeps it bushy. Oregano is unusual in that it tastes even stronger once dried.
hardiness_notes_seasoned: Oregano is a hardy perennial. Common oregano (Origanum vulgare) is the hardiest, reliably perennial to about zone 4 with sharp drainage and, at the cold edge, a winter mulch; Greek oregano (subsp. hirtum), the best culinary type, is a touch less hardy, to about zone 5. Most types are reliable in roughly zones 5 to 9, with zone 3 grown as an annual or a bring-in container plant, and tender types like Syrian oregano hardy only in the warmest zones. Good drainage matters as much as cold: oregano rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it, and it also struggles in hot, humid climates.
hardiness_notes_beginner: Oregano is tough and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 for the hardiest common type with good drainage and a winter mulch). Greek oregano, the best for cooking, is a little less cold-hardy. In the very coldest areas (zone 3), grow it for one season or in a pot you bring inside. Just as important as cold: oregano hates wet feet and will rot in soggy soil, and it also struggles in hot, humid places.
year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper off, pinch the tips at about 6 inches to build a bushy plant, and harvest only lightly. Oregano establishes fairly quickly and reaches full size by about the second year, after which it produces steadily for several years before it should be divided or replaced. Watch for and contain any spread from the start.
year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting established. Water it fairly regularly until it settles in, then cut back, pinch the tips when it is about 6 inches tall to make it bushy, and only pick a little. Oregano fills out by about year two, then produces well for several years before you replace or divide it. Keep an eye on its spreading from the start.
soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Work only a little coarse compost into lean soil, and on heavy clay improve drainage with a raised bed or mound rather than digging in sand, which can worsen clay. Aim for lean, neutral to slightly alkaline ground; oregano is intolerant of acidic soil, so lime sour ground lightly, and it does not want rich soil.
soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. Mix only a little coarse compost into the soil. If your ground is heavy clay, plant oregano in a raised bed or mound instead, because that drains better. The goal is poor soil that is neutral to slightly chalky, not rich soil; if your soil is acidic, add a little garden lime.
bloom_time_beginner: Oregano flowers in mid-to-late summer, with tiny white, pink, or purple flowers that bees and butterflies love. The leaves taste best just before it blooms, so many gardeners pinch the flowers off. When yours flowers depends on where you live.
bloom_time_seasoned: Oregano blooms in mid-to-late summer, carrying small clusters of white, pink, or purple flowers that are a strong pollinator draw. Leaf flavor peaks just before the flowers open, so many growers pinch or cut the buds to favor the leaves. Exact timing shifts with your region and is set per zone.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, oregano dies back to the ground and goes dormant. Hold off on watering and feeding, leave any hard cutback for spring, and at the cold edge of its range apply a loose winter mulch of straw or evergreen boughs after the ground freezes, removing it as growth resumes. A resting plant needs almost no water, and it is wet soil, not the cold itself, that most often kills oregano over winter.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Where winters freeze, oregano dies back and rests through the cold months. Stop watering and feeding it, save any big trim for spring, and in the coldest areas lay a loose winter mulch of straw over it after the ground freezes, taking it off in spring. A resting plant barely needs water, and it is usually soggy soil, not the cold, that kills oregano over winter.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Oregano is grown for its leaves, not for fruit, so no cross-pollination planning is needed and a single plant is fine. Its small summer flowers are self-fertile and are a strong draw for bees, butterflies, and moths, a bonus for the garden. Note that letting flowers set seed is how oregano self-sows and spreads, so deadhead if you want to limit it.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one oregano plant, and you do not need a partner plant, because oregano is grown for its leaves rather than fruit. Bees and butterflies love its little flowers, but if you let those flowers make seed, oregano will spread itself around, so cut them off if you want to keep it in check.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: After the summer flowers fade, shear off the spent flower stems and cut the plant back into leafy growth to spur a fresh flush, avoiding the bare old wood, which resprouts poorly. Deadheading now also limits self-seeding. Frequent harvesting plus this post-bloom shear keeps oregano bushy; even so, plants go woody with age and are best divided or replaced every few years, with old leggy wood cut out at the end of winter.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Once the summer flowers fade, trim off the old flower stems and cut the plant back into its leafy growth for fresh new leaves, avoiding the hard woody stems. Trimming now also stops it dropping seed everywhere. Snipping oregano often plus this trim keeps it bushy, but it still gets woody with age, so replace or divide it every few years and cut out old woody stems at the end of winter.
